paragraphs: The FOURTH class comprises the following miscellaneous powers:
1. A power "to promote the progress of science and useful arts, by securing, for a limited time, to authors and inventors, the exclusive right to their respective writings and discoveries."

Few will question the usefulness of this power. In Great Britain the courts have solemnly ruled that an author's copyright is a right of common law. The right to useful inventions seems, for equally good reasons, to belong to the inventors. In both cases the public good fully agrees with the claims of individuals. The States cannot separately make effective provision for either, and most of them have already acted ahead of the question, passing laws at Congress's request.

2. "To exercise exclusive legislation, in all cases whatsoever, over such district (not exceeding ten miles square) as may, by cession of particular States and the acceptance of Congress, become the seat of the government of the United States; and to exercise like authority over all places purchased by the consent of the legislatures of the States in which the same shall be, for the erection of forts, magazines, arsenals, dockyards, and other needful buildings."

The need for complete authority at the seat of government is so plain that it proves itself. Every legislature in the Union, and I might say in the world, exercises such a power by virtue of its general supremacy. Without it, public authority might be insulted and its proceedings interrupted with impunity. Worse, the members of the general government would have to depend, for protection while doing their duty, on the State that contains the seat of government. That might expose the national councils to a charge of being overawed or influenced, which would dishonor the government and displease the other members of the Confederacy. The point carries more weight because public improvements would gradually pile up at the government's permanent home. That would be too great a public pledge to leave in the hands of a single State, and it would create so many obstacles to moving the government that its necessary independence would be curtailed further. The federal district is small enough to satisfy any jealousy of the opposite kind. And every imaginable objection seems to be met, for several reasons. The district is to be set aside for this use with the consent of the State that cedes it. The State will no doubt provide in the compact for the rights and consent of the citizens living there. The inhabitants will find enough in their own interest to become willing parties to the cession. They will have had a voice in electing the government that will exercise authority over them. They will of course be allowed a municipal legislature for local purposes, chosen by their own votes. And the authority of the State legislature, and of the inhabitants of the ceded part of the State, to agree to the cession will come from the whole people of the State, through their adoption of the Constitution.

A like authority over forts, magazines and the like, set up by the general government, is just as plainly necessary. The public money spent on such places, and the public property kept in them, require that they be exempt from the authority of the particular State. Nor would it be proper for places on which the security of the whole Union may depend to be dependent in any degree on one member of it. All objections and scruples are again met by requiring the agreement of the States concerned in every such establishment.
3. "To declare the punishment of treason, but no attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood, or forfeiture, except during the life of the person attained."

Since treason may be committed against the United States, the authority of the United States ought to be able to punish it. But new-fangled and artificial treasons have been the great engines with which violent factions, the natural offspring of free government, have usually taken turns venting their malignity on each other. The Convention has therefore shown great judgment in setting up a barrier against this particular danger. It has put into the Constitution a definition of the crime, fixed the proof required for conviction and forbidden Congress, even when punishing treason, to carry the consequences of guilt beyond the person who committed it.

4. "To admit new States into the Union; but no new State shall be formed or erected within the jurisdiction of any other State; nor any State be formed by the junction of two or more States, or parts of States, without the consent of the legislatures of the States concerned, as well as of the Congress."

The articles of Confederation contain no provision on this important subject. Canada was to be admitted as of right when she joined in the measures of the United States, and the other COLONIES, by which were plainly meant the other British colonies, at the discretion of nine States. The compilers of that document seem to have overlooked the eventual creation of NEW STATES. We have seen the problem this omission caused, and the assumption of power it led Congress into. The new system has therefore, and very properly, filled the gap. The general precaution, that no new States be formed without the agreement of the federal authority and of the States concerned, accords with the principles that ought to govern such transactions. The particular precaution against creating new States by splitting a State without its consent calms the jealousy of the larger States, just as the matching precaution against merging States without their consent calms that of the smaller ones.

5. "To dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting the territory or other property belonging to the United States," with a proviso that "nothing in the Constitution shall be so construed as to prejudice any claims of the United States, or of any particular State."

This is a power of very great importance, and the same kind of considerations that show the propriety of the previous one call for it. The proviso attached to it is proper in itself, and was probably made absolutely necessary by jealousies and disputes over the Western territory that are well enough known to the public.

6. "To guarantee to every State in the Union a republican form of government; to protect each of them against invasion; and on application of the legislature, or of the executive (when the legislature cannot be convened), against domestic violence."

In a confederacy founded on republican principles and made up of republican members, the superintending government clearly ought to have authority to defend the system against aristocratic or monarchical innovations. The closer such a union is, the more interest the members have in one another's political institutions, and the greater their right to insist that the forms of government under which they entered the compact be SUBSTANTIALLY kept. But a right implies a remedy; and where else could the remedy be placed than where the Constitution places it? Governments of unlike principles and forms have proved less suited to any sort of federal coalition than governments of a similar nature. "As the confederate republic of Germany," says Montesquieu, "consists of free cities and petty states, subject to different princes, experience shows us that it is more imperfect than that of Holland and Switzerland." "Greece was undone," he adds, "as soon as the king of Macedon obtained a seat among the Amphictyons." In the latter case, no doubt, the new member's disproportionate strength, as well as its monarchical form, had a share in bringing about the events. It may possibly be asked what need there could be for such a precaution, and whether it might become a pretext for altering the State governments without the States' own agreement. These questions have ready answers. If the interposition of the general government should not be needed, the provision for such an event will be only a harmless superfluity in the Constitution. But who can say what experiments the caprice of particular States, the ambition of enterprising leaders, or the intrigues and influence of foreign powers may produce? To the second question, the answer is that if the general government steps in under this constitutional authority, it will of course be bound to stay within the authority. But the authority reaches no further than a GUARANTY of a republican form of government, which assumes that a government of the form to be guaranteed already exists. So as long as the States keep their existing republican forms, the federal Constitution guarantees them. Whenever the States choose to put other republican forms in their place, they have a right to do so and to claim the federal guaranty for the new ones. The only restriction on them is that they may not exchange republican for antirepublican Constitutions, a restriction that, it is presumed, will hardly be thought a grievance.

Every society owes its parts protection against invasion. The broad wording used here seems to protect each State not only against foreign hostility but also against ambitious or vengeful schemes by its more powerful neighbors. The history of confederacies, ancient and modern, proves that the weaker members of a union should not be indifferent to the wisdom of this article.

Protection against domestic violence is added just as properly. It has been noted that even among the Swiss cantons, which strictly speaking are not under one government, provision is made for this object. The history of that league shows that mutual aid is often asked for and given, by the most democratic cantons as much as by the others. A recent and well-known event among ourselves has warned us to be ready for emergencies of the same kind.

At first glance it might seem not to fit republican theory to suppose either that a majority lacks the right to overthrow a government or that a minority will have the force to do so; and so it might seem that federal interposition could never be required except when it would be improper. But theoretical reasoning, here as in most other cases, has to be qualified by what practice teaches. Why could illicit combinations for violent purposes not be formed by a majority of a State, especially a small State, just as they could by a majority of a county or district within the same State? And if the State's authority ought to protect the local officials in the second case, ought not the federal authority to support the State authority in the first? Besides, some parts of the State constitutions are so interwoven with the federal Constitution that a violent blow to one cannot be struck without wounding the other. Insurrections in a State will rarely lead to federal interposition unless the number involved bears some proportion to the friends of government. It will be far better for the superintending power to put down the violence in such cases than for the majority to be left to defend its cause in a bloody and stubborn contest. The existence of a right to interpose will generally spare the need to use it.

Is it true that force and right are necessarily on the same side in republican governments? May the smaller party not have such an advantage in money, in military talent and experience, or in secret help from foreign powers that it also wins an appeal to the sword? May a more compact and advantageous position not tip the scale its way against a larger number so situated that it is less able to bring its strength to bear promptly and together? Nothing could be more fanciful than to imagine that in a trial of actual force victory can be calculated by the rules that hold in a census of the inhabitants or that settle the outcome of an election! May it not happen, in short, that the minority of CITIZENS becomes a majority of PERSONS, through the addition of alien residents, a chance crowd of adventurers, or people whom the constitution of the State has not admitted to the right to vote? I pass over an unhappy class of people, numerous in some of the States, who in the calm of regular government are sunk below the level of men, but who in the stormy scenes of civil violence may rise into the human character and give a superiority of strength to any party they may join.

Where it is doubtful on which side justice lies, what better umpires could two violent factions desire, as they rush to arms and tear a State to pieces, than the representatives of confederate States, who are not heated by the local flame? They would combine the impartiality of judges with the affection of friends. How happy it would be if all free governments could enjoy such a remedy for their infirmities, and if an equally effective plan could be established for the universal peace of mankind!

Suppose it is asked what remedy there would be for an insurrection that spreads through all the States and commands a superiority of the entire force, though it has no constitutional right. The answer must be that such a case would lie beyond the reach of human remedies, and fortunately it also lies beyond the reach of human probability. It is recommendation enough for the federal Constitution that it lessens the risk of a calamity for which no possible constitution can supply a cure.

Among the advantages of a confederate republic that Montesquieu lists, an important one is "that should a popular insurrection happen in one of the States, the others are able to quell it. Should abuses creep into one part, they are reformed by those that remain sound."

7. "To consider all debts contracted, and engagements entered into, before the adoption of this Constitution, as being no less valid against the United States, under this Constitution, than under the Confederation."

This can be taken only as a declaratory proposition. Among other reasons, it may have been inserted to reassure the foreign creditors of the United States, who cannot be strangers to the pretended doctrine that a change in the political form of civil society magically dissolves its moral obligations.

Among the lesser criticisms leveled at the Constitution, it has been remarked that the validity of engagements ought to have been asserted in favor of the United States as well as against them. In the spirit that usually marks little critics, this omission has been blown up into a plot against the national rights. The authors of this discovery can be told what hardly anyone else needs telling: engagements are by nature reciprocal, so asserting their validity on one side necessarily implies their validity on the other; and since the article is merely declaratory, establishing the principle in one case is enough for every case. They can be told further that every constitution must confine its precautions to dangers that are not altogether imaginary, and that there is no real danger that the government would DARE, with this constitutional declaration before it or even without it, to cancel debts justly owed to the public on the pretext they condemn here.
8. "To provide for amendments to be ratified by three fourths of the States under two exceptions only."

That experience would suggest useful changes had to be foreseen. A way of making them therefore had to be provided. The way the Convention preferred seems to bear every mark of propriety. It guards equally against two extremes: too much ease, which would make the Constitution too changeable, and too much difficulty, which might make its discovered faults permanent. It also lets the general government and the State governments equally start the amendment of errors, whichever side experience may expose them on. The exception in favor of equal suffrage in the Senate was probably meant as a safeguard for the residuary sovereignty of the States, which that principle of representation in one branch of the legislature implies and secures; and the States particularly attached to that equality probably insisted on it. The other exception must have been admitted on the same grounds that produced the privilege it protects.
9. "The ratification of the conventions of nine States shall be sufficient for the establishment of this Constitution between the States, ratifying the same."

This article speaks for itself. Only the express authority of the people could give the Constitution proper validity. Requiring the unanimous ratification of the thirteen States would have put the essential interests of the whole at the mercy of the caprice or corruption of a single member. It would have shown a lack of foresight in the Convention that our own experience would have made inexcusable.

Two very delicate questions present themselves here. 1. On what principle can the Confederation, which stands as a solemn compact among the States, be replaced without the unanimous consent of its parties? 2. What relation is to exist between the nine or more States that ratify the Constitution and the remaining few that do not become parties to it?

The first question is answered at once by turning to the absolute necessity of the case, to the great principle of self-preservation, and to the transcendent law of nature and of nature's God, which declares that the safety and happiness of society are the aims of all political institutions and that all such institutions must be sacrificed to them. PERHAPS an answer can also be found without looking beyond the principles of the compact itself. We have already noted, among the defects of the Confederation, that in many of the States it received no higher sanction than a mere ratification by the legislature. The principle of reciprocity seems to require that its binding force on the other States be brought down to the same level. A compact between independent sovereigns, resting on ordinary acts of legislative authority, can claim no higher validity than a league or treaty between the parties. It is an established doctrine about treaties that all the articles are conditions of one another; that a breach of any one article is a breach of the whole treaty; and that a breach by either party frees the others and authorizes them, if they wish, to declare the compact violated and void. Should it unhappily become necessary to appeal to these delicate truths to justify going ahead without the consent of particular States to dissolving the federal pact, will the complaining parties not find it hard to answer the MULTIPLIED and IMPORTANT infractions that may be thrown back at them? There was a time when we all had to veil the ideas this paragraph sets out. The scene has now changed, and with it the part that the same motives dictate.

The second question is no less delicate, and the pleasing prospect that it will remain merely hypothetical forbids an overcurious discussion of it. It is one of those cases that must be left to provide for itself. In general, it may be observed that although no political relation can exist between the assenting and the dissenting States, the moral relations will remain in force. The claims of justice on both sides will hold and must be met. The rights of humanity must always be respected on both sides. And it is hoped that considerations of common interest, and above all the memory of the dear scenes now past and the hope of a speedy victory over the obstacles to reunion, will not urge in vain MODERATION on one side and PRUDENCE on the other.
